sentences.text: The office was under the root of a beech on the boundary bank, and Orla got into it the way everybody gets into these things, which is by losing something and being unreasonable about it.
The thing she had lost was a watch.
It had been her grandfather's, it had come to her in April when he died, it had not worked since about 2011, and she had worn it every day since the funeral on a strap that was four holes too big.
She lost it in the wood on the ninth of October, and she knew exactly where, and it was not there.
She knew exactly where because she had felt it go.

She had been climbing the bank at the far end by the stile, had put her hand down into the bracken to steady herself, and had felt the strap slide over her knuckles — a sensation so specific that she had stopped and looked at her wrist before she had even finished thinking about it.
Four holes too big.
She had been meaning to have a hole punched in it since May.
She went back twenty times.
She took a rake.
She took a metal detector belonging to a neighbour, which found two bottle tops and a horseshoe and put her in a very bad mood.

On the twelfth visit, in November, in the rain, she was on her hands and knees under the beech on the boundary bank with her arm down a hole between two roots, and something the other end took hold of her sleeve and pulled twice.
The hole was not on the bank by the stile.
It was two hundred metres away and she had no reason to be at it except that she had by then searched everywhere with a reason and had started on the places without one.
She did not scream.
She has thought about this since with a certain amount of pride.

What she did was take her arm out very slowly and sit back and look at the hole, and the hole looked back at her, and after a moment a badger came about a third of the way out of it and stopped, with its stripes on and its nose going, at a distance of perhaps forty centimetres.
It considered her for a while.
Then it went back down, and there was a sound like a drawer, and it came up again with something in its mouth and put it on the leaf mould between them.
It was a bottle top.
It was, she saw when she picked it up, quite an old one — the crimped kind, rusted right through in one place, with a lettering on the top that had gone.

Orla, who had had a very frustrating month, said, "That's not mine." The badger looked at the bottle top, and looked at her, and made a noise in its throat that she has never been able to describe and has never mistaken for anything else since, and went back down the hole.

She sat under that tree in the rain for another quarter of an hour, and when nothing else happened she went home and did not tell anybody, and came back on the Saturday with a torch and a good deal of nerve.
